title: Dunleavy orders state probe of Peltola campaign over same-name Senate challenger - Whatfinger News Quick Hits
text:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a criminal investigation into Mary Peltola’s Senate campaign after reports that allies helped recruit a same-name challenger to confuse voters backing Sen. Dan Sullivan.
Dunleavy directed the Alaska Department of Public Safety on Wednesday to examine whether the reported recruitment effort broke state law and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted, following a CBS News report on the New York Times account of the episode.
The governor said the Alaska Division of Elections had already looked into the matter. He framed the new probe as a defense of basic ballot integrity in a ranked-choice Senate race that already features four candidates on the general-election ballot.
At the center of the dispute is Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher listed with no party affiliation, sharing the first and last name of incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Republicans have called the second Sullivan a sham candidate meant to siphon votes. He has denied that charge and said he is genuinely interested in running.
Dunleavy says deliberate voter confusion hits election integrity
In a social media post ordering the Department of Public Safety review, Dunleavy did not say much about what he believes is at stake.
“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support. Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”
He instructed investigators to determine “whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted.” The New York Post reported the governor’s directive as a formal step toward possible charges tied to the decoy-candidate allegations.
Peltola, the Democratic Senate candidate, called the coverage a distraction at a campaign stop in Soldotna. She said voters are focused on costs, not ballot lineups.
“Nobody’s waking up worried about ballot composition. Not even me. I’m worried about my bills. I’m worried about affordability in health care.”
Her campaign spokesman said the campaign “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign” and cast her candidacy as a fight to lower costs and put Alaska first. The Democratic Senate Campaign Committee likewise said it “is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan.”
Times reporting and text messages put operatives in the frame
The New York Times reported that people aligned with Peltola’s campaign helped recruit the same-name candidate, and that a Democratic operative who worked with her campaign and national Democrats helped encourage Daniel J. Sullivan to run, citing text messages and interviews. The paper described the move as appearing to be part of a wider effort to draw more candidates into the race.
Nate Adams, spokesman for Sen. Dan Sullivan’s campaign, said the denials no longer hold.
“Mary Peltola and her campaign have spent months gaslighting Alaskans, denying a scheme they were running all along. Alaskans deserve the truth.”
State officials had earlier tried to keep the second Sullivan off the ballot, arguing he was trying to confuse voters and that his was not a good-faith candidacy. The Alaska Supreme Court rejected that effort and ruled he can appear. The ballot identifies the sitting senator as a Republican and the incumbent; the other Sullivan carries no party label. Voters may rank the four remaining candidates rather than pick only one, a system Trump has urged Alaska voters to scrap as stacked against clear outcomes.
The Washington Examiner noted the investigation lands as pressure mounts just days before Election Day, with the Times account prompting sharper calls to remove the disputed names from the ballot.
Trump demands prosecution and flags election fraud
President Trump told reporters he thinks Peltola and the other Sullivan should be prosecuted. On Truth Social he went further.
“I don’t think Mary Peltola, after perpetrating such a terrible scheme, should be allowed to run, because this is ELECTION FRAUD. The Democrats cheated!”
Breitbart reported Trump also said, “They said they didn’t do it, and they did do it, and they got caught,” calling it “voter fraud at the highest level,” while noting early voting had already begun. A former aide’s account of campaign awareness of the tactic added to the political heat surrounding the probe.
Last week the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the election if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses because of voter confusion over the dueling Sullivans. Attorney General Todd Blanche described the filing as an effort to “put guardrails in place.” Trump told reporters, “Well, I’m the one that said, ‘Do it.’” That action fits a broader pattern of DOJ moves to stop Alaska certification tied to the second Sullivan.
House Oversight Chairman James Comer has opened a separate congressional inquiry, sending letters seeking interviews with former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios and operative Jerid Kurtz over the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan, Just the News reported.
“Democrats are the party of fraud. Knowing they can’t win on the issues, Democrats schemed to rig the U.S. Senate election in Alaska by deliberately confusing voters.”
Democrats have answered election-related probes with legal pushback in other fights, including cases where party lawyers mobilized as the Trump DOJ challenged results in multiple states. The DSCC, for its part, pointed to past Republican efforts to recruit or prop up candidates and cited a 2024 Alaska House run by a man serving a 20-year prison sentence in New York, plus an Arizona man who entered this year’s Alaska Senate primary.
What the ballot and the probes leave unresolved
Four candidates advanced from Alaska’s nonpartisan primary earlier this year. For months the same-name challenger has drawn Republican fire. Dunleavy’s Department of Public Safety order now tests whether any of the recruitment conduct crossed into criminal or civil violations under state law.
Peltola’s team continues to deny involvement. Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. continues to insist his candidacy is real. The Times account, the governor’s investigation, Comer’s letters, and the Justice Department’s certification suit all keep the same core question in front of voters: whether a same-name entry on a ranked-choice ballot was encouraged to scramble clear choice.
Trump’s public demand for prosecution and removal sits alongside the state’s own law-enforcement track and the federal lawsuit already filed, a stacked accountability map that leaves little room for the “distraction” label to settle the matter. Similar high-stakes Alaska fights have drawn direct presidential attention before, including when Trump issued onstage pardons for Alaska diesel shop owners caught in federal cases.
When campaigns play name games with the ballot, voters are the ones left holding the bag, and governors who order real investigations are doing the job the public expects.
